title: Negative: a consumed, regrowing fuel neither caps the size of catalysis-induced condensates nor makes them divide or form shells; starving the cores makes bodies 2x larger and coarsening faster than with a fuel reservoir
summary: The question predicted that bodies larger than the fuel penetration length l_F would starve in the core and so stop growing, splitting (Zwicker) or turning into shells (Bergmann). In the CIPS world of 20261025T1845-c23-cips-metabolic-claim, three regimes on 2 seeds each: reservoir (F held at 1), fed (DF=1, kF=0.2, bodies R_eq~3.5 px, about l_F) and starved (DF=0.05, kF=0.5, y=3, l_F~1 px, bodies R_eq~6 px, fuel rim/core 15). In every arm the body count keeps falling through merges (coarsening.png): at t=3000 the reservoir arm has 167-170 bodies (mean area 57-58 px), fed 190-192 (50 px), starved 82-93 (104-119 px), and starved keeps coarsening to 71-81 by t=4000 with the 95th-percentile body area still rising (200 -> 218-266 px). Splits: 0-2 per run vs 106-232 merges (persistent splits 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0). The enzyme never forms a shell: e rim/core 0.86 (starved) and 0.95 (fed), no holes, because the product diffuses into the starved core and keeps the enzyme there. dispersion.py adds that the question's suggested fed arms (chi=0.3, kF 0.01-0.05) are linearly stable: fuel depletion turns CIPS off. The fed arm sits slightly below the reservoir in body size, so the consumed fuel slows coarsening a little but does not arrest it within t=3000.

finding.operator: consumed, regrowing fuel F_t = DF lap F - y kc F e (1-p) + kF (1-F) feeding catalysis-induced phase separation of a conserved enzyme
finding.control: matched reservoir twin (F held at 1; pack_hold1, pack_pa_hold), same seeds and grid
finding.result: t=3000 body count: reservoir 167-170, fed 190-192, starved 82-93 (2 seeds each); starved 71-81 at t=4000 vs reservoir 148-149; persistent splits 0-2 against 106-232 merges in every run; enzyme rim/core 0.86-0.95 (no shells)
